case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal employee reservist activated to active duty under 10 U.S.C. § 12301(d) is entitled to differential pay under USERRA when their activation occurs during a presidentially declared national emergency, thereby qualifying as active duty under 10 U.S.C. § 101(a)(13)(B).
case_analysis.legal_provision: 10 U.S.C. § 101(a)(13)(B), which defines 'active duty during a war or national emergency' for purposes of triggering differential pay entitlements under the Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act (USERRA); also 10 U.S.C. § 12301(d), governing voluntary activation of reservists.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Nick Feliciano argues that a reservist called to active duty under Section 12301(d) while a presidentially declared national emergency is in effect has, by plain statutory language, been ordered to active duty 'under a provision of law during a national emergency,' thus satisfying Section 101(a)(13)(B) and entitling him to differential pay from the Department of Transportation/FAA. Feliciano further contends that his activation orders expressly invoked a presidential emergency declaration, strengthening his claim, and that the Federal Circuit's contrary interpretation is irreconcilable with the statute's plain text and congressional intent to protect and compensate reservists called into service.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The Department of Transportation, represented by the Solicitor General, argues that activation under Section 12301(d) — a voluntary consent-based provision — does not automatically qualify as active duty 'during a national emergency' for differential pay purposes under Section 101(a)(13)(B), and that the Federal Circuit correctly denied the claim. The government also raises procedural and vehicle concerns, noting that Feliciano failed to raise specific arguments about the nature of his service before the Federal Circuit, that key legal issues were not pressed or passed upon below, and that Feliciano never formally requested differential pay from the FAA nor submitted required documentation, making this case a poor vehicle for resolving the broader statutory question.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas's most serious argument — that 'under any other provision of law during a national emergency' requires the activation authority itself to be tethered to emergency-related legal frameworks — remains unpersuasive against the plain text, and Justice Gorsuch's invocation of Ressam v. United States, 553 U.S. 272 (2008), confirms that 'during' carries temporal rather than causal meaning as a matter of this Court's own precedent. I am gratified that Justice Alito has moved to the petitioner's side, though I share his instinct that the narrowest possible holding is most appropriate here — we should hold only that activation under § 12301(d) during a presidentially declared national emergency satisfies § 101(a)(13)(B)'s plain text, and remand on the documentation and procedural questions rather than resolving them. As Chief Justice, I would assign the majority opinion with an eye toward a narrow, text-focused holding that commands the broadest coalition and avoids broader pronouncements about USERRA's full scope or the administrative record questions Justice Alito correctly flags. Justice Thomas's structural canon-against-surplusage argument is interesting but ultimately proves too much — the catch-all 'any other provision of law' must do independent work beyond the enumerated provisions, and reading it to require emergency-nexus activation would collapse it into the very provisions it was meant to supplement.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch's invocation of Ressam v. United States, 553 U.S. 272 (2008), ultimately proves dispositive for me as a textualist: if this Court has already established that 'during' denotes temporal coincidence rather than causal relationship, intellectual consistency demands I apply that same meaning here rather than selectively deploying a different reading when it favors the government. My prior concern that 'under' does independent work requiring an emergency-nexus is weakened by Justice Barrett's observation that the statute presents two grammatically distinct conditions — the provision of law (§ 12301(d)) and the temporal circumstance (a declared national emergency) — and conflating them imports a nexus requirement Congress did not write. I remain genuinely troubled by the vehicle concerns I raised, and I would insist on a narrow holding with remand on the documentation and exhaustion questions rather than resolving those issues here, consistent with Justice Alito's approach. The canon against surplusage argument I advanced cuts less cleanly than I initially believed, because the catch-all 'any other provision of law' does independent work by sweeping in authorities Congress could not enumerate in advance, and the Federal Circuit's judicially-invented nexus requirement rewrites unambiguous statutory text in a manner inconsistent with originalist methodology.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas's most serious argument — that 'under any other provision of law during a national emergency' requires the activation authority itself to be tethered to emergency purposes, not merely temporally coincident with a declared emergency — remains the strongest challenge to my position, but I cannot sustain it as a textualist after Ressam. As Justice Gorsuch correctly notes, this Court has already held that 'during' denotes temporal coincidence, and intellectual consistency forbids me from applying that word's meaning differently here simply because the result favors a servicemember rather than the government. Justice Thomas's surplusage argument — that reading 'during' as purely temporal renders the enumerated specific provisions redundant with the catch-all — has some force, but the enumerated provisions do independent work by specifying particular authorities with their own procedural requirements, so the catch-all sweeping in additional authorities does not render them superfluous. I maintain my preference for a narrow remand that leaves the documentation and exhaustion questions for further development, consistent with my concern that we not resolve significant statutory questions on underdeveloped records.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas's textualist argument that 'during a national emergency' functions as a limiting condition requiring the activation authority itself to be tethered to emergency authority is the strongest opposing argument, but it ultimately fails because it reads 'under any other provision of law' and 'during a national emergency' as a single fused requirement rather than as two distinct statutory elements — the provision of law (§ 12301(d)) and the temporal circumstance (a declared national emergency) — which is the more natural grammatical reading. Justice Gorsuch's invocation of Ressam v. United States is persuasive here: this Court has already held that 'during' denotes temporal coincidence, not causal relationship, and we cannot selectively apply that interpretive principle only when it favors the government. Justice Alito's vehicle concerns deserve serious consideration, but as Justice Kagan correctly notes, they go to remedy and remand scope rather than the core statutory question — and the Federal Circuit's Adams framework, however nonprecedential, creates real interpretive uncertainty that disadvantages servicemembers in precisely the circumstances USERRA was designed to protect. The pro-veteran canon, combined with the canon against surplusage that would render 'any other provision of law' largely meaningless under the government's reading, reinforces my conclusion that Feliciano's activation satisfies § 101(a)(13)(B)'s plain text.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas's most refined argument in Round 2 — that 'under' does real work requiring activation pursuant to an emergency-related legal framework, not merely contemporaneous with one — is the strongest remaining challenge, but it still cannot overcome the plain text. The statute says 'under any other provision of law during a national emergency': § 12301(d) is the provision of law Feliciano was activated under, and the national emergency declaration satisfies the temporal condition 'during.' Justice Thomas's reading would require us to import a nexus requirement between the activating authority and the emergency that the text simply does not contain, and as Justice Gorsuch correctly emphasizes, Ressam's holding that 'during' denotes temporal coincidence is binding and cannot be selectively applied only when it favors the government. I am also persuaded by Justice Jackson's structural point that the catch-all 'any other provision of law' was Congress's deliberate choice to avoid exhaustive enumeration — Justice Thomas's surplusage argument actually cuts the other way, because if the catch-all were limited to emergency-nexus authorities, it would largely duplicate the enumerated provisions rather than supplement them. Justice Alito's conversion to the petitioner's side on the core statutory question, while maintaining his procedural concerns as going to remedy rather than merits, reflects the correct analytical framework, and I would join a narrow opinion reversing the Federal Circuit on the textual question and remanding on documentation and exhaustion issues.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas raises the most serious counterargument — that 'during a national emergency' functions as a limiting condition on the nature of the activation authority rather than a mere temporal marker — but this reading cannot survive the plain text. The statute says 'any other provision of law during a national emergency,' and § 12301(d) is unquestionably 'a provision of law'; if Congress had intended to require that the activating authority itself be emergency-specific, it would have written 'under any other provision of law enacted for or pursuant to a national emergency,' not the broad temporal formulation it chose. As I noted in my own analysis, Ressam v. United States, 553 U.S. 272, 274 (2008), confirms that 'during' denotes temporal coincidence, and Justice Thomas's reading effectively renders the catch-all phrase 'any other provision of law' superfluous — the enumerated provisions already cover emergency-specific authorities, so the catch-all must sweep more broadly or it does no independent work. Justice Alito's vehicle concerns deserve respect, but the Federal Circuit did resolve the statutory interpretation question below, and the core textual error warrants correction even if remand is appropriate for the administrative documentation issues.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas's most serious challenge — that 'under any other provision of law during a national emergency' requires the activation authority itself to be tethered to emergency-specific legal frameworks, not merely temporally coincident with a declared emergency — remains the strongest opposing argument, but it cannot survive the plain text read alongside Ressam v. United States, 553 U.S. 272 (2008). As Justice Gorsuch correctly emphasizes, Ressam establishes that 'during' denotes temporal coincidence, and intellectual consistency demands we apply that settled meaning here rather than selectively deploying it only when it favors the government. Justice Thomas's surplusage canon argument — that the enumerated specific provisions would be rendered redundant if the catch-all sweeps in all temporally coincident activations — actually cuts the other way: the enumerated provisions cover specific emergency-activation statutes, while the catch-all captures the broader universe of activations under any provision of law that happen to occur during a declared emergency, giving each clause independent work to do. I join Chief Justice Roberts's minimalist approach: hold narrowly that § 12301(d) activation during a presidentially declared national emergency satisfies § 101(a)(13)(B)'s plain text, and remand on the documentation and procedural questions Justice Alito correctly identifies as underdeveloped.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas raises the most serious challenge to my position, arguing that 'during' functions as a limiting condition on the nature of the call rather than a mere temporal marker, and that § 12301(d)'s consent-based character means it operates independently of emergency authority. But this argument conflates two distinct statutory questions: what kind of activation authority is invoked (§ 12301(d)) versus when that authority is exercised (during a declared national emergency). The text of § 101(a)(13)(B) asks whether activation occurred 'under any other provision of law during a national emergency' — and § 12301(d) is unquestionably 'a provision of law,' while the temporal condition 'during a national emergency' is satisfied by the existence of a presidential declaration at the time of activation, as Ressam confirms 'during' denotes temporal coincidence. Justice Alito's vehicle concerns deserve serious weight, but as Justice Kagan correctly notes, the procedural deficiencies go to remedy and remand scope rather than the core statutory interpretation question, and the Federal Circuit's framework — however nonprecedential — creates ongoing interpretive uncertainty that warrants correction rather than avoidance.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas's most refined argument in Round 2 — that 'under' does independent work requiring the activation to be pursuant to an emergency-related legal framework, not merely contemporaneous with one — is the strongest remaining challenge, but it cannot overcome the plain text. As Justice Gorsuch correctly emphasizes, § 12301(d) is unquestionably 'a provision of law,' and the statute's structure places 'during a national emergency' as a temporal modifier on when the activation occurs, not as a qualifier on what kind of law authorizes it; Congress knew how to write a nexus requirement and chose not to. Justice Thomas's surplusage argument — that a purely temporal reading renders the enumerated specific provisions redundant with the catch-all — actually cuts the other way: the enumerated provisions ensure coverage regardless of whether a national emergency has been declared, while the catch-all extends protection to any statutory authority exercised during a declared emergency, giving each clause independent work to do. I am also persuaded by Justice Alito's evolution on this question: his procedural concerns are real and should shape the remedy (a narrow remand on documentation and exhaustion questions), but they do not undermine the core statutory holding that the Federal Circuit's judicially-invented nexus requirement rewrites unambiguous text in a manner that punishes voluntary service during national emergencies — precisely the conduct USERRA was designed to encourage.

John Roberts.reasoning: The plain text of 10 U.S.C. § 101(a)(13)(B) defines active duty as service 'under a provision of law during a national emergency,' and as this Court held in Ressam v. United States, 553 U.S. 272 (2008), the word 'during' carries a temporal rather than relational meaning — the government cannot now argue the opposite position it successfully advanced in Ressam without undermining basic principles of statutory consistency. While I am sympathetic to the vehicle concerns raised by the Solicitor General under United States v. Williams, 504 U.S. 36, 41 (1992), the Federal Circuit did resolve the claim below, and the core statutory interpretation question — whether temporal coincidence with a national emergency suffices under § 101(a)(13)(B) — was necessarily implicated even if not fully developed. Consistent with my preference for narrow rulings, I would resolve this case on the limited ground that activation under § 12301(d) during a presidentially declared national emergency satisfies the plain text of § 101(a)(13)(B), without reaching broader questions about what documentation or procedural steps are required to perfect a differential pay claim, leaving those issues for remand. USERRA's protective purpose for reservists further counsels against reading in a substantive nexus requirement that Congress did not write into the statute.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Applying strict textualism and the original public meaning of 10 U.S.C. § 101(a)(13)(B), the phrase 'under any other provision of law during a war or during a national emergency' requires that the activation authority itself be tied to the declared emergency — the temporal modifier 'during a national emergency' functions as a limiting condition on the nature of the call or order, not merely a calendar coincidence. Section 12301(d) is a consent-based voluntary activation authority that operates independently of any emergency declaration; the mere fact that a national emergency happened to be in effect at the time of activation does not transform a voluntary, consent-based order into one issued 'under' emergency authority. Furthermore, the procedural deficiencies are significant from an originalist standpoint respecting institutional competence: Feliciano never formally requested differential pay from the FAA nor submitted required documentation, and key arguments were not pressed or passed upon below, consistent with the principle articulated in United States v. Williams, 504 U.S. 36, 41 (1992), that this Court should not reach issues not properly preserved. The government's reading better respects the statutory structure Congress deliberately constructed, which expressly enumerated specific activation authorities and added others over time, suggesting that Section 12301(d) voluntary activations were not intended to automatically qualify absent a direct nexus to emergency authority.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: As a textualist, I am genuinely troubled by the Federal Circuit's apparent addition of a 'contingency operation' requirement not found in the plain text of § 101(a)(13)(B) or § 5538(a), and I take seriously the argument that the statute's plain language may support Feliciano's position. However, the procedural deficiencies here are substantial and dispositive at the certiorari stage: Feliciano failed to press the specific argument about his activation orders' express invocation of an emergency declaration before the Federal Circuit, meaning the issue was neither pressed nor passed upon below under United States v. Williams, 504 U.S. 36, 41 (1992). Furthermore, Feliciano never formally requested differential pay from the FAA nor submitted the required military orders and leave and earnings statements, meaning the administrative record is incomplete and the case presents no concrete, fully-developed dispute for this Court to resolve. While I would be open to granting certiorari in a better-postured vehicle to correct what may well be an atextual Federal Circuit interpretation, this case's procedural infirmities make it an inappropriate vehicle for resolving the broader statutory question, and the practical consequence of issuing a ruling on an underdeveloped record could create administrative chaos for federal agencies calculating differential pay obligations.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The plain text of 10 U.S.C. § 101(a)(13)(B) defines active duty 'under a provision of law during a national emergency,' and Feliciano's activation under § 12301(d) during a presidentially declared national emergency satisfies that definition on its face — the voluntary nature of § 12301(d) does not negate the statutory text's requirements, which speak to the circumstances of activation, not its consensual character. The government's procedural vehicle concerns, while not frivolous, do not overcome the substantive statutory question, particularly where Feliciano's activation orders expressly invoked the emergency declaration. Under the well-established pro-veteran canon articulated in King v. St. Vincent's Hospital, Fishgold v. Sullivan Drydock, and Coffy v. Republic Steel Corp., any genuine ambiguity in USERRA's differential pay provisions must be resolved in the servicemember's favor, consistent with Congress's manifest remedial purpose to protect reservists from financial hardship during service. Denying differential pay to a reservist whose orders were issued during a declared national emergency would create precisely the kind of inequity USERRA was designed to prevent, penalizing those who answered the call to serve.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The plain text of 10 U.S.C. § 101(a)(13)(B) defines a contingency operation to include activation 'under any other provision of law during a war or during a national emergency declared by the President or Congress,' and the word 'during' is most naturally read as a temporal modifier establishing contemporaneity — not a requirement that the activating provision itself be emergency-specific. Section 12301(d) is unquestionably 'a provision of law,' and when Feliciano's activation orders expressly invoked a presidential emergency declaration and occurred while such a declaration was in effect, the statutory text is satisfied on its face. The government's reading would render the catch-all phrase 'any other provision of law' largely superfluous by requiring the activating statute to independently tether to emergency authority, which conflicts with the canon against surplusage and the pro-veteran interpretive principle that ambiguities in benefits statutes should be resolved in favor of the servicemember. While the vehicle concerns about exhaustion and documentation are not trivial, they go to remedy and remand scope rather than the core statutory question, and the Federal Circuit's nonprecedential ruling below created interpretive uncertainty that warrants this Court's correction.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The plain text of 10 U.S.C. § 101(a)(13)(B) uses the word 'during,' which this Court has consistently held denotes a temporal link — 'at the same time as' — not a substantive or causal relationship, as confirmed in Ressam v. United States, 553 U.S. 272, 274 (2008). The Federal Circuit's requirement of a 'sufficiently close connection' between the reservist's service and the national emergency is a judicial rewrite of unambiguous statutory text, substituting the court's policy preferences for Congress's chosen words — precisely the kind of interpretive overreach I have consistently rejected. The statute says 'any other provision of law during a war or national emergency,' and § 12301(d) is unquestionably 'a provision of law'; if a presidentially declared national emergency was in effect at the time of activation, the temporal condition is satisfied by its plain terms. Furthermore, the canon favoring veterans and servicemembers — a longstanding interpretive principle — reinforces this reading, and it would be perverse to reward involuntary activees with differential pay while denying it to those who voluntarily stepped forward to serve during the same emergency.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The plain text of 10 U.S.C. § 101(a)(13)(B)'s catchall provision — 'any other provision of law during a war or during a national emergency declared by the President or Congress' — most naturally reads as requiring only temporal coincidence with a declared national emergency, not a causal nexus between the emergency and the activation authority invoked. The word 'during' is a temporal connector, and courts should not redraft statutory text to impose requirements Congress did not include, particularly when doing so disadvantages reservists who voluntarily serve during emergencies compared to those involuntarily activated. While I take seriously the government's vehicle concerns regarding Feliciano's failure to press certain arguments below and his procedural shortcomings in requesting differential pay from the FAA — concerns that give me some pause about whether this is the ideal vehicle — the Federal Circuit's interpretation in Adams and its application here represents a departure from the statute's plain meaning that warrants correction. The practical workability of a provision-by-provision textual inquiry, rather than the Federal Circuit's fact-intensive post hoc nexus analysis, also better serves the institutional values of predictability and administrability that Congress likely intended when enacting USERRA's protections for uniformed service members.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The plain text of 10 U.S.C. § 101(a)(13)(B)'s catchall provision — 'any other provision of law during a war or during a national emergency declared by the President or Congress' — most naturally reads 'during' as establishing a temporal condition, not a causal or substantive nexus requirement. As a textualist, I am bound to apply the ordinary public meaning of statutory language, and as this Court recognized in United States v. Ressam, 553 U.S. 272, 274-275 (2008), 'the term during denotes a temporal link' — that is its most natural meaning. The Federal Circuit's gloss requiring an unspecified 'connection' to the emergency effectively rewrites the statute's broad catchall language, substituting the court's policy judgment for Congress's deliberate textual choice to use expansive language after enumerating specific provisions. While the government's vehicle concerns about preservation and failure to formally request differential pay from the FAA carry some weight, they do not overcome the fundamental statutory interpretation error below, and the Federal Circuit's nonprecedential but binding-on-remand Adams framework warrants correction.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The plain text of 10 U.S.C. § 101(a)(13)(B)'s catch-all provision encompasses 'any other provision of law during a war or during a national emergency declared by the President or Congress,' and Section 12301(d) is unambiguously 'a provision of law' — the Federal Circuit's judicially-invented 'connection' requirement and voluntary/involuntary distinction appear nowhere in the statutory text and constitute impermissible judicial rewriting of congressional enactments. As a matter of procedural fairness and practical consequence, denying differential pay to reservists who volunteer during declared national emergencies creates a perverse disincentive precisely when the military most needs skilled personnel to step forward, undermining USERRA's core protective purpose under 38 U.S.C. § 4311(a). The Federal Circuit's reliance on ejusdem generis to limit the catch-all provision to involuntary activations is unpersuasive because the temporal modifier 'during a national emergency' does independent work in the statute, and Congress's remedial intent in USERRA counsels liberal construction in favor of servicemembers. While the government's vehicle concerns about exhaustion and documentation have some merit, they go to remedy and remand scope rather than the core statutory interpretation question this Court should resolve.

John Roberts.reasoning: The unanimity of my colleagues across methodological lines — from Justice Thomas's originalism to Justice Sotomayor's purposivism to Justice Gorsuch's textualism — reinforces my confidence that the plain meaning of 'during' as temporal coincidence is correct, and that the government's nexus requirement is an unauthorized judicial insertion. Justice Kagan's structural observation remains the most persuasive to me as Chief Justice: a statutory scheme that rewards involuntary activations under § 12301(a) while denying differential pay to volunteers under § 12301(d) serving during the same declared emergency produces an incoherence that the text does not compel and institutional credibility counsels against perpetuating. As I noted in my prior reasoning, the vehicle concern about Feliciano's failure to formally request differential pay is real, but Justice Kavanaugh correctly identifies that this goes to remedy and remand instructions rather than the underlying statutory entitlement — and resolving the legal question now provides workable guidance for the many federal employee reservists facing this uncertainty. I will assign the majority opinion with instructions to hold narrowly on temporal coincidence while explicitly reserving documentation, exhaustion, and the precise scope of the pro-veteran canon for remand, thereby preserving the Court's institutional credibility through a minimalist ruling that commands the broadest possible consensus.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: I find myself in substantial agreement with Justice Gorsuch's formulation, which most closely tracks my own originalist and textualist methodology: the plain ordinary meaning of 'during' as confirmed in Ressam admits of only one natural reading — temporal coincidence — and the government's nexus requirement is a judicial invention that adds words Congress never wrote. Justice Roberts raises the most significant concern about vehicle problems, particularly Feliciano's failure to formally request differential pay, but as Justice Kavanaugh correctly notes, those procedural deficiencies go to remedy and remand rather than the underlying statutory entitlement, and the core legal question is squarely presented. The structural argument Justice Barrett identifies — that Congress deliberately chose broad temporal language for the catchall after enumerating thirteen specific provisions — further confirms that the Federal Circuit's causal nexus requirement cannot be reconciled with the statute's text or structure. My confidence increases slightly from 0.85 to 0.90 given the unanimity of my colleagues' textual analysis, though I note that unanimity itself is not a reason to change one's position; the text simply compels this result.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The unanimity of my colleagues across methodological lines — from Justice Thomas's originalism to Justice Sotomayor's purposivism — confirms what the plain text already compels: 'during' means temporal coincidence, full stop. Justice Gorsuch puts it most precisely: the government's nexus requirement commits the cardinal sin of adding words Congress never wrote, and after Ressam's clear gloss on 'during,' that interpretive move is simply unavailable to us. The government's strongest remaining argument — that § 12301(d) voluntary activations are categorically different — founders on the same textual rock, because Congress used 'during' without any voluntariness qualifier and could have written 'pursuant to' or 'because of' if it wanted causation. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that we should hold narrowly on the temporal coincidence question and remand the vehicle concerns — Feliciano's failure to formally request differential pay — to the Federal Circuit for resolution of exhaustion and documentation issues rather than allowing those procedural deficiencies to obscure the correct statutory answer.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I am gratified that my colleagues across the ideological spectrum have converged on the plain-text reading of 'during' as a purely temporal modifier, consistent with Ressam. Justice Gorsuch's point that the government's position requires judicially inventing a 'connection' requirement that Congress never wrote is particularly well-taken — as someone who approaches statutory interpretation from a different methodological starting point than Justice Gorsuch, I reach the same destination through the additional lens of USERRA's remedial purpose: denying differential pay to reservists who answered their country's call during a declared national emergency would undermine the very economic protections Congress enacted to ensure servicemembers are not penalized for their service. The government's strongest argument — the vehicle concern about Feliciano's failure to formally request differential pay — is real but, as Justice Kavanaugh correctly notes, it goes to remedy and remand instructions rather than the underlying statutory entitlement, and should not prevent us from resolving the legal question that creates ongoing uncertainty for federal employee reservists. I write separately to emphasize that the pro-veteran canon is not merely a tiebreaker but an affirmative interpretive principle reflecting Congress's consistent solicitude for those who bear the burdens of military service, and that the Federal Circuit's distinction between 'voluntary' and 'involuntary' mobilizations is not only textually unsupported but practically harmful to the working-class reservists USERRA was designed to protect.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: I find myself in substantial agreement with my colleagues across the ideological spectrum, which itself is telling — when textualists like Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch reach the same destination as purposivists like Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson, the statutory text is doing real work. Justice Gorsuch's point that the government's position requires reading limiting language into the statute that Congress simply did not write is exactly right, and I would add my own structural observation: the catchall's function in § 101(a)(13)(B) is precisely to sweep in activations that don't fit the enumerated provisions, and imposing a nexus requirement would gut that function by demanding that the catchall activation authority itself be emergency-related — which would make it redundant with the enumerated provisions. The strongest argument for the government is the vehicle concern about Feliciano's failure to formally request differential pay, which Justice Roberts wisely flags, but as Justice Kavanaugh correctly notes, that goes to remedy and remand instructions rather than the underlying statutory entitlement. I would hold narrowly that temporal coincidence with a declared national emergency satisfies § 101(a)(13)(B), while leaving exhaustion and documentation questions for remand.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: I am gratified that my colleagues across the ideological spectrum have converged on the same textual conclusion, and I find Justice Thomas's formulation particularly apt: importing a causal nexus requirement into 'during' is a 'cardinal sin under textualism' because it adds words Congress simply did not write. The government's strongest counterargument — that reading 'during' as purely temporal would allow any activation under any provision of law to qualify so long as some emergency declaration happens to be in effect somewhere — is not without force, but it proves too much; Congress could have written 'pursuant to' or 'in connection with' a national emergency if it wanted a causal nexus, and the fact that it chose 'during' after Ressam's clear gloss on that word forecloses the government's rewrite. Justice Kagan's structural point also resonates with me: the government's interpretation produces the perverse result of rewarding involuntary activations under § 12301(a) while denying differential pay to volunteers under § 12301(d) who serve during the same declared emergency, an incoherence that the text does not compel and that the pro-veteran canon counsels against. I would hold narrowly that temporal coincidence with a presidentially declared national emergency satisfies § 101(a)(13)(B), consistent with Chief Justice Roberts's preference for a limited ruling, and remand for resolution of the administrative exhaustion and documentation questions.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The conference has reached a remarkable unanimity that I find genuinely persuasive on the merits rather than merely as a matter of consensus. Justice Gorsuch's formulation remains the most textually precise: 'during' as interpreted in Ressam admits only a temporal reading, and the government's causal nexus requirement requires us to substitute 'pursuant to' or 'in connection with' for language Congress actually chose — an interpretive move we have no authority to make. Justice Kagan's structural observation about the catchall's function is particularly compelling from my institutionalist perspective: a nexus requirement would gut the catchall by making it redundant with enumerated provisions, producing exactly the kind of incoherent statutory structure that undermines the Court's credibility as a faithful interpreter of congressional text. The government's strongest remaining argument — the vehicle concern about Feliciano's failure to formally request differential pay — is real, and I would join Chief Justice Roberts in favoring narrow remand instructions that preserve those administrative exhaustion questions for the lower courts rather than resolving them in the first instance here.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: After careful review of my colleagues' arguments in this second round of deliberation, I find the textual case for the petitioner has only strengthened. Justice Gorsuch's formulation remains the most precise articulation of why the government's position fails: importing a causal nexus requirement into the word 'during' is precisely the kind of judicial rewriting of statutory text that textualism forbids, and Congress's choice of 'during' after Ressam's clear gloss on that word as a purely temporal modifier is dispositive. The government's strongest remaining argument — that reading 'during' as purely temporal would allow any activation under any provision to qualify so long as some emergency declaration is in effect somewhere — is not without surface appeal, but as Justice Gorsuch correctly notes, it proves too much: Congress had available the words 'pursuant to' or 'in connection with' if it wanted causation, and its deliberate choice of 'during' must be given operative effect.
